techniques.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows. The schtasks utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel. In some cases, adversaries have used a .NET wrapper for the Windows Task Scheduler, and alternatively, adversaries have used the Windows netapi32 library and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to create a scheduled task. Adversaries may also utilize the Powershell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod`, which leverages WMI class `PS_ScheduledTask` to create a scheduled task via an XML path. An adversary may use Windows Task Scheduler to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence.

detections.name: Detection of Suspicious Scheduled Task Creation and Execution on Windows

analytics.description: Detects the creation, modification, or deletion of scheduled tasks through Task Scheduler, WMI, PowerShell, or API-based methods followed by execution from svchost.exe or taskeng.exe. Includes detection of hidden or anomalous scheduled tasks, especially those created under SYSTEM or suspicious user contexts.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system. PowerShell can also be installed on Linux and macOS. Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including Empire, PowerSploit, PoshC2, and PSAttack.

analytics.description: Detects behavioral chains where PowerShell is launched with encoded commands, unusual parent processes, or suspicious modules loaded, potentially followed by network connections or child process spawning. Supports detection of both direct (powershell.exe) and indirect (.NET automation) invocations.

playbook.title: Response Playbook for Malicious Scheduled Task Creation on HR-LAPTOP-22
playbook.executive_summary: A scheduled task "OneDriveUpdateCore" was created by user CORP\a.khan on HR-LAPTOP-22 using PowerShell to run an encoded payload as SYSTEM at every logon, indicating high‑severity persistence. Immediate containment, evidence collection, eradication of the task, and system hardening are required.

detection_and_analysis.action: Collect volatile memory and process list from HR-LAPTOP-22
detection_and_analysis.detail: Use a trusted forensic tool (e.g., FTK Imager) to capture RAM and enumerate running processes, focusing on any powershell.exe or taskeng.exe instances.

detection_and_analysis.action: Query Windows Event Logs for related events
detection_and_analysis.detail: Search WinEventLog:Security for EventID 4698 and Sysmon EventID 1 for the task creation time; also review WinEventLog:PowerShell for encoded command execution.

detection_and_analysis.action: Identify the full encoded PowerShell command
detection_and_analysis.detail: Extract the Base64 string from the scheduled task definition and decode it in a sandbox to determine payload behavior.

containment.action: Disable the scheduled task "OneDriveUpdateCore" on the host
containment.detail: Run schtasks /Change /TN "OneDriveUpdateCore" /Disable and verify status with schtasks /Query /TN "OneDriveUpdateCore".

containment.action: Isolate HR-LAPTOP-22 from the corporate network
containment.detail: Move the endpoint to a quarantine VLAN or disable its network adapter to prevent further execution of the payload.
Use taskkill /PID <pid> for powershell.exe instances launched with -enc flag; confirm parentage via Process Lineage Analysis.

eradication.detail: Run schtasks /Delete /TN "OneDriveUpdateCore" /F after confirming no legitimate task shares the name.

eradication.action: Remove the encoded PowerShell script from the system
eradication.detail: Search for the decoded script file or temporary files in %TEMP% and delete them; ensure no remnants remain.

eradication.action: Reset the user account permissions for CORP\a.khan
eradication.detail: Review group membership and remove unnecessary privileged rights; enforce least‑privilege.

recovery.action: Restore system integrity from a known good backup
recovery.detail: Reimage HR-LAPTOP-22 or apply a clean system state snapshot after confirming eradication steps succeeded.

recovery.action: Re‑enable network connectivity and monitor for re‑creation of the task
recovery.detail: Place the host back on the network with enhanced logging; alert on any new scheduled task creation events.

hardening.action: Enable Application Allowlisting for scheduled tasks
hardening.detail: Configure Windows Defender Application Control to only allow signed binaries for task actions, blocking arbitrary PowerShell execution.

hardening.action: Audit and enforce privileged account usage
hardening.detail: Implement M1026 controls and enable detailed logging for SYSTEM account task creation; review audit logs daily.

hardening.action: Deploy detection rule DET0441 across all endpoints
hardening.detail: Ensure the scheduled task creation detection rule is active and tuned to flag hidden or anomalous tasks.
